title: Bihar's GomatiRoots Turns Homemade Badi Into Brand, Wins Shuru Kar Funding
excerpt: Shital Kumari's Patna startup, built around Bihar's traditional lentil badi, has received Rs 1 lakh through YourStory's Shuru Kar initiative after recording Rs 32 lakh in revenue in its first financial year.
body:
• GomatiRoots, founded by Shital Kumari in Patna, has received Rs 1 lakh in funding through YourStory's Shuru Kar initiative, from YourStory founder Shradha Sharma.
  • The startup sells traditional Bihari badi and related foods in more than 50 stores in Patna and on Amazon, Flipkart and JioMart, and recorded Rs 32 lakh in revenue in its first financial year.
  • Some products are made with rural women's self-help groups, and Kumari is in discussions with JEEViKA, Bihar's rural livelihoods initiative, on longer-term sourcing partnerships.
  • For readers: GomatiRoots products can be ordered through the marketplaces named above and the company's own website, as listed in the YourStory report.

Shital Kumari attended the Bihar Idea Festival in Patna in September 2025 with questions and no business. Nearly a year later, her startup GomatiRoots, which packages Bihar's traditional lentil-based badi as a branded food product, has received Rs 1 lakh in funding through YourStory's Shuru Kar initiative. The funding came from Shradha Sharma, founder and chief executive of YourStory and The Bharat Project, according to YourStory. The festival where Kumari first encountered the programme was launched by YourStory under The Bharat Project, in collaboration with the Bihar Industries Department and the Chandragupt Institute of Management, Patna.

From a family kitchen to a company

The idea came from loss. After her mother died during the Covid-19 pandemic, Kumari looked for badi that tasted like the one her mother used to make and could not find it, YourStory reported. Some products raised concerns about adulteration, and others did not offer the varieties she wanted. Researching the market, she found established brands for pickles and papad but no comparable identity for badi, a food eaten regularly in Bihar and many other parts of India with lentils and vegetables.

"There are several pickle and papad brands, but I did not see the same kind of identity for badi."

Kumari's route into business was through a state scheme. She applied under the Bihar Laghu Udyami Yojana, the state support programme for small entrepreneurs listed on the Bihar government's Udyami portal, and received Rs 50,000 as a first instalment and Rs 1 lakh as a second instalment, along with training, YourStory reported. She added a loan of Rs 2 lakh and founded GomatiRoots in Patna. Before that, after moving to Patna to support her younger siblings, she had worked in video editing, taught children and sold lychees while preparing for the Union Public Service Commission examination.

What the company sells, and where

GomatiRoots started with badi and now sells urad dal badi, moongori, chana dal badi, Bihari masala badi and kohrauri, as well as fryums including tisiyori and tilauri, according to YourStory. The company supplies retail stores, restaurants and cloud kitchens and sells directly to customers. Its products are in more than 50 stores in Patna, it is working on distribution in other districts of Bihar, and it also sells through exhibitions, fairs and canopy stalls.

The operating problem is seasonality. Traditional badi production depends on sunlight and weather, which can affect output and quality. Kumari told YourStory the company has worked on its production methods so customers receive consistent quality through the year, and that repeat orders from retail shopkeepers have been an early sign of demand. Maintaining that consistency in production, packaging and storage is the condition for entering larger retail networks, she said.

Women producers and the next market

Part of the range is prepared with rural women's self-help groups, including tisiyori made with flaxseed, potatoes and rice, and rice-based tilauri and kohrauri. Kumari was invited as a buyer to the Saras Mela and is in discussions with JEEViKA about sourcing directly from its members, with the aim of fair prices and regular income, YourStory reported. She also wants to work with Bihar farmers so the lentils used for badi are grown locally.

What's next

Kumari said the Rs 1 lakh from Shuru Kar will be used for working capital and marketing. Her stated plans are to enter larger retail networks and quick-commerce platforms, strengthen e-commerce and direct-to-consumer sales, formalise operations and licences, and increase production capacity. Over the next three to five years, she aims to take GomatiRoots beyond Bihar into major Indian cities, open the company's own store and eventually export. Those are ambitions stated to YourStory, not yet results: the test ahead is whether a seasonal, home-made food can hold its quality and supply at the scale larger retailers require.
